statement: The final system designed in this session is the newly unread message indicator, a feature seen day in and day out on social platforms such as LinkedIn, Twitter, Facebook and Instagram.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now the final system for today is with design, newly unread indicator.

statement: Scenario for the indicator: you are offline, you receive a message, and when you log in the next time you see a counter of it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You receive a message and when you log in the next time, you see the counter of it.

statement: The teacher demonstrated the indicator live on Instagram (LinkedIn and Twitter had no new messages), because it is something everyone sees every day but typically takes for granted.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because it's something that we see every day. But we typically take it for granted.

statement: A badge showing 3 on the message icon means three NEWLY unread messages, not three unread messages.
detail: The teacher was not sure when he last checked Instagram; the 3 is about new arrivals, not the total unread backlog.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: These are not three unread messages. These are three newly unread messages.

statement: Clicking the message icon makes the count drop to zero, but that does not mean the messages were read; it only means the user acknowledges that messages are present, and the unread messages are still there.
detail: In the live demo the badge did not behave exactly as the teacher wanted, but the idea is that the count should reduce to zero on click.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It does not mean that I have read the messages. It just means that I am acknowledging that I have messages.

statement: In the Instagram demo, clicking the icon made the badge disappear even though hundreds of unread messages remained; the badge never shows a total such as 99, 10,000 or 50,000 unread messages.
detail: The teacher clicked a conversation ('Flying taxi') during the demo; the count disappeared while many conversations stayed unread.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Unread messages are there, but this does not mean that here I would say 99 or 10,000 or 50,000.

statement: The user can choose not to read the messages at all; the indicator only signals that there are new unread messages.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you can choose not to read the message, but it indicates that there are new unread messages.

statement: The newly unread indicator design is used to introduce a very interesting high-level pattern.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There is a very interesting high level pattern that I want to introduce through the system.

statement: Requirement: inform the user about the presence of new messages; the wording is chosen carefully - presence of new messages, not unread and not unacknowledged.
detail: Clicking the icon resets the counter to zero whether or not the messages were read.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Terminology, like the words that are used very carefully, presence of new messages, not unread, not unacknowledged.

statement: Twisted requirement (a pseudo constraint added by the teacher): the badge number is the count of unique people you have new messages from, not the count of newly unread messages - e.g. 300 messages from three unique people shows 3.
detail: When the user clicks the message icon, the count disappears irrespective of whether the user read the messages.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it indicates that you have messages from three unique people.

statement: Requirements list: near real-time update; update when a message is received; number of newly unread = number of unique people from whom messages were received.
detail: Board wording: '# new unreads = # different people from which message received and is unread'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Requirements: near real-time update, message when received,

statement: "Newly" means since the last time the user clicked the message icon.
detail: The turn also contains 'less than 24 hours'; per the transcript flag the first clause may belong to Student 3, so the 24-hour reading may be a student proposal that the teacher replaced with 'since the last click on the message icon'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: newly means less than 24 hours, that is last time when I clicked on the message icon, since then.
flags: check: first clause may be Student 3 (diarization lag)
check: speaker of 'less than 24 hours' - possibly Student 3's proposal refined by the teacher to 'since last click'

statement: First approach proposed by a student: track whether each message is read, track the user's last read time (when the message icon was last tapped), and filter messages by last read time to count the unique users who messaged, to populate the badge.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: there should be a kind of a filtering mechanism based on the last read time, so that I can get the number of unique users

statement: Messages data model for the first approach: each message with its text, from user, to user and timestamp; the timestamp is critical, and the teacher added the from and to columns.
detail: Board: table msgs (msg, from, to, ts.), later renamed messages.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: I want to start with a data model, like the message data model, that is received from the message itself, and the time stamp

statement: A second data model stores each user's last read time, needed to compute the count.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: And a time stamp, and then there should be another data model which would be like last read time.

statement: A student jumped to a message queue with the user subscribed to it, partitioned on the from user; the teacher stepped back to ask first what the input to the system is and what the messages table actually stores.
detail: No verdict on the queue idea itself; the teacher redirected to the data model.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Let's go step back. What is the input to the system?

statement: A student first said storing all messages a user ever received does no harm but would not be a scalable solution.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: I can store. There's no harm in storing, but I think that would not be a scalable solution.

statement: In the first approach the messages table stores all messages sent to the user (text, from, to, timestamp); its scale is pretty huge, which the teacher deferred.
detail: The teacher pressed: if user B sends a message to user A, the table must store either all the messages or part of them; the student settled on all messages ever sent to the user.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So the text part from this to this and times. Okay. You have that messaging table. So now the scale of this is pretty huge
flags: check: possible teacher interjections inside Student 3's turn at 02:10:50

statement: The last-read data is kept in a user activity table: a one-to-one mapping with the user, one entry per user storing last_read_at and other details.
detail: The student first called it a 'latest message' metadata table; the teacher suggested something more substantial because you might want to store more. Board: user (id); user_activity (user_id, last_read_at).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: let's just store it in a user activity. It's basically one-on-one mapping with user.

statement: A student's query proposal: select messages where timestamp > last_read_at and order them; the teacher corrected that ordering is pointless because only the count is rendered, not the messages.
detail: Student's proposal: 'select from messages where timestamp is greater than last read at ... I need to order them'.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: You are not, you don't want to send a message. You just want to render the count. Why order?

statement: SELECT * FROM messages WHERE to = user AND timestamp > last_read_at (assuming a join with user activity) returns one row per message, so three messages from one sender give three rows, while the requirement is the number of unique senders.
detail: The student explained the problem: 'if I send three messages to you ... three rows ... But I don't want three rows as input. I just want one.'
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You're doing select star from messages. Yeah. Where to is equal to your user and timestamp is greater than last read at.

statement: The crude query for the badge: SELECT COUNT(UNIQUE(from)) FROM messages WHERE to = <user id> AND ts > last_read_at.
detail: Board: 'Select count(uniq(from)) from ... where to = ? & ts > last_read_at'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Select count unique from from messages where to is equal to your ID and.

statement: A student said the problem with the query is indexing and proposed indexing messages on timestamp alone; the teacher pointed out this sorts all data across all users by timestamp, and then gave a composite index instead.
detail: Student: 'timestamp would be a good indexing factor because we want all the messages after time this time'. Correction: composite index starting with to (see the composite-index item).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So it will be like across all users, all data is sorted by timestamp.

statement: Even indexed, the count query is expensive: if a user has received 10,000 messages you go through 10,000 rows and then take the unique of them, on every page load; with millions of users active at any moment, firing this query is super expensive.
detail: The teacher was not doubting correctness: 'System would work, but at millions of people ... firing this query is super expensive.'
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now imagine doing it every time the page loads. Very expensive.

statement: Index for the crude query: a composite index on (to, from, timestamp), so all entries of a given 'to' are clubbed together, grouped by 'from' and ordered by timestamp; filtering then goes directly to where the 'to' of interest starts.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So all the entries of to will be clubbed together, then grouped by from and then ordered by timestamp.

statement: A student suggested the composite index order (to, timestamp, from) instead; the teacher agreed, because with timestamp second the scan can easily be cut short.
detail: Teacher: 'Because if you do, then you can very easily cut short. So it will be to, timestamp.'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: I think it should be to, timestamp and from, right?

statement: Worst case even with the best field order: if one user sent you 10,000 messages, the query iterates 10,000 index entries only to find the unique count is one (or two or three); squeezing performance by rearranging index fields does not remove this cost.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You're going to 10,000 index entries to eventually figure out that the unique count is just one or two or three or something like that.

statement: A student proposed keeping a separate table with just a count instead of scanning messages, since what matters is whether messages are being sent, not their content; the teacher agreed this leads to a more efficient implementation.
detail: Teacher: 'So you don't care about the actual messages. So now we are coming to a more efficient implementation of it.'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: We can have another table that tells how many messages have been sent. Just a count.

statement: The count query over the messages table is a crude way, not an incorrect way: it is not very efficient but it is very correct.
detail: Board: box 'CRUDE' pointing at the tables; pink 'INEFFICIENT' next to the query.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is a crude way of building things, which gives you, which is not very efficient but very correct.

statement: The messages table is the source of truth for messages and the user activity table is the source of truth for when the user last clicked the message icon, so the query always gives an exactly (100%) correct count of unique senders; its only problem is inefficiency - it iterates over all of a user's messages to find the unique ones.
detail: Teacher's framing question: 'do we really need to iterate through all the messages of a user that it received and then figure out, okay, these are the unique ones? Can we do better?'
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It will be 100 correct no matter what. But the problem is it is just a little, a little, not a little, but rather inefficient.

statement: A student proposed dropping the relational query and using a non-relational database: per user key, a hash map holding a total count; the teacher clarified the count is a named key (renamed newly unread count), not a nested hash table.
detail: Teacher: 'Count with a number. What do you mean count with a number? ... Then is this even a hash table?' Board: 'user_id: { count, count }' then 'newly_unread_count: 3'. The 02:19:57 fragment may be the teacher noting that a similar query would be fired in a non-relational database too.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Instead of this, I will try to go with non-relational database
flags: check: speaker of "database because like similar query you'll fire there" (02:19:57, Teacher?)

statement: The student added a unique-users set (a set of senders) to the per-user record next to the newly unread count; the teacher asked what the difference between the count and the set is, since the set already identifies unique senders.
detail: Teacher: 'What is the difference between this and this? ... Isn't that what set was supposed to be?' Board: 'unique_users: set<>' with 'newly_unread_count: 3' later struck through.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: And in this hash map also we are also having one other hash map, that is unique users. It's kind of like a set actually

statement: Refined proposal: keep just a unique-user set per user and show the length of the set on the notification badge; the teacher asked whether the separate count is really needed, and it was dropped.
detail: Teacher: 'Do you really need this?'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Basically we can have a, just a unique user set.

statement: Every set keeps track of its own length, so getting the size of a set is O(1); a separate count is unnecessary.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Everyone keeps, every set gives a track of the length of the set.

statement: Whenever a user messages this user, the sender is put into the recipient's unique-users set.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: whenever any user, user, like, messages this user ID, it will just, it will just put the user in that set.

statement: When the user clicks the message icon, the set is deleted; the deletion is O(1), making this system much more efficient.
detail: Board: 'user_id: unique_users set<>' / 'delete set when user clicks [icon] icon'.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: whenever you user click that button, we can just delete this thing.

statement: A classic way to build almost any system: you either query the source of truth, or you keep things pre-computed.
detail: The teacher addressed everyone: you would see this in almost every single system you implement.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You either can query the source of truth, or you can keep things pre-computed.

statement: Query the source of truth directly when you need strong consistency; to get more efficiency, pre-compute the data or store it in a form that is directly consumable.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Either you directly fire source of truth when you need strong consistency, or you may build, or to get more efficiency, you may pre-compute...

statement: With the pre-computed set you directly get its length as the number of unique senders, while the source-of-truth approach fires an expensive query - whether implemented in SQL or NoSQL does not matter.
case_study: Newly unread indicator: set length vs count(unique(from)) query.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Here you had to fire an expensive query, SQL, NoSQL implementation, anything, that does not matter.

statement: The cost of pre-computing: keeping the pre-computed data updated becomes our responsibility and needs another flow that also writes the data there, whereas the source of truth is updated by nature because all messages are ingested into it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: now it's our responsibility to keep this updated. Here it was by nature, it was updated because it is actually the source of truth.

statement: Neither approach is wrong; it depends on what you prioritise and your scale: for a startup querying the source of truth works just fine, but as millions of people become concurrently active you may be tempted to go with the pre-computed approach.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: As a startup, this would work just fine for you folks.

statement: A student proposed a NoSQL store because a variable-length list of user IDs is kept against each user ID: a document or key-value store such as MongoDB, with key = user ID and value = a set of user IDs.
detail: The teacher accepted the key-value-with-set idea but used Redis as the example store.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: key is the user ID and value is a set where each element is a user ID.

statement: Use Redis for the per-user set (chosen as an oversimplification because almost everyone knows it); any key-value store that offers a set as the value works - the key highlight is reusing the database's set functionality so you don't have to check-and-set yourself.
detail: Board: 'K.value store / value is set / Redis'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Any key-value store that gives you set functionality in the value so that you don't have to check and set and whatnot

statement: Read path: a get status API talks to Redis, counts the elements of the user's set and returns the count to render on the badge.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It might be a get status API, which what it would do is it would talk to this Redis and count the elements...

statement: Clear path: a clear API goes to Redis and deletes the user's key when the message icon is clicked; with get and clear, the read path and a very trivial write path are done.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So we have clear API. It goes to Redis and it deletes the key that we just said.

statement: The interesting part is the write path: someone has to put into Redis the unique senders from whom the user received messages while offline.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now comes the interesting part, that how will you update this Redis with this data that you need.

statement: The client must be smart: if the user is already on the messaging tab, a message arriving (even in another conversation) should not count as newly unread, so no badge update is needed.
detail: The teacher called the student's input 'brilliantly put'.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: if the user is already on the messaging tab, even though he is reading some other users message...
flags: check: "Correct, correct. So the client also is offline, yeah." may be a teacher interjection

statement: With a WebSocket connection for messaging, the backend can check whether the socket connection with the client is off and only then update Redis (e.g. when the user is watching reels rather than on the messaging tab).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: backend can check that if the socket connection with the client is off, then I can update the Redis.

statement: The design needs not just one database but a few more databases to support it, which is where the high-level pattern comes in.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because it's not just one database that we would have, we would have a few more databases to support it.

statement: The input to the system is the messaging service, because it knows when a message could not be delivered to the user.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because our messaging service knows when a message is not sent to the user

statement: Simplification: here the count is updated only when the user is offline; in the real world the count also increases when you are on another tab, and you can add such cases - whatever the definition of 'unsent' (not on the tab, offline, doing something else), it comes from the messaging service.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now whatever your definition of unsent is, user not on the tab, user offline or user doing something else, right?
flags: unclear: "very other use case as a very well explained"

statement: The messaging service is the source of truth for delivery because it knows whether a message was delivered, whether the user is on the tab, and whether the WebSocket connection is up.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: messaging service would know if the message is delivered to you or not, if you are on that tab or not...

statement: The messaging service either takes help of an online/offline indicator service or has the information itself, because all persistent connections are with its edge servers, which know whether the user is online, offline, connected, or on which tab.
detail: Board: 'Websockets - know if a user is connected or not, we use this to find the undelivered messages'; 'or ONLINE/OFFLINE service'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So that edge server is the one that would know if you're online or offline or connected or not, or on which tab.
flags: check: sentence may start mid-way, words before "help of" possibly lost

statement: 'On message unsent' is an umbrella event covering every case where we want to pop the notification; the if/else logic of where the user is and what they are doing is implemented in the messaging layer.
detail: Board: 'ON_MSG_UNSENT'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I'm creating an umbrella of everything that I want to pop notification on into this message called on message unsent.

statement: On-message-unsent events flow into Kafka and become the input to the system; each event says which user sent which message to whom, and consumers add the sender to the recipient's set (to track unique users), typically stored in Redis.
detail: Board: each event contains { src: "A", dest: "B", msg }; 'user_id : {u1, u2, u5}', 'B: {C, D}'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now this, all of this comes to this Kafka on message unsent, which becomes the input to our system.

statement: Any key-value database that is partitionable by default (all of them are) and provides a set as value can hold the unique-sender sets.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can pick any key-value database, which is partitionable by default. All of them are, and provide set as value, any database.

statement: Full design so far: read path - get status counts the set length, clear status deletes the set when the user clicks the message button; write path - on-message-unsent events from the messaging service (using online/offline info) are consumed by workers that write the new sender into the Redis cluster.
detail: Board: READ Path -> Status check API (get_status / clean_status) -> Redis Cluster; WRITE Path: ON_MSG_UNSENT -> Status update workers -> Redis Cluster; Notification System.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: your consumers consume it and writes to this Redis cluster that, hey, new user, new user, user, you received a new message

statement: Many people would stop designing once there is a read path and a write path, considering the design converged - but that is not good enough here.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Lot of people would stop designing over this stage.

statement: The Redis cluster is overburdened: it serves a huge number of reads (millions of users refreshing or moving between pages call the get API), plus a large number of writes when users click the message icon, plus an update on every message-unsent event.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Plus anytime there is message unsend, you are updating into this database. This database is overburdened.

statement: The database is the most brittle component of an infrastructure, so check whether you are doing unnecessary operations on it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: as I always say, database is the most brittle component of an infrastructure.

statement: The get status path is already the bare minimum: you must go to the database because it is the source of truth, and a read replica is not needed because it is an in-memory DB anyway.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You have to go to the database, read it, read replica. You don't need it. It's an in-memory DB anyway.

statement: The clear status path must delete the key and cannot be reduced; it does no unnecessary operation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Clear status. You have to go and delete the key over here. You can't do much over there.

statement: The write path does unnecessary work: because the value is a set, whether user B sends one message or 10,000, the database state changes only on the first message; for the other 9,999 writes nothing changes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If I receive one message from user B or 10,000 message from user B, my message, the state of my database is not changing...

statement: When you are offline, friends do not send just one message; they send 5, 10, 15, 20 or 30 short messages ('Hey, what are you doing? Come here. We are going for this.').
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When you are offline, they don't send you just one message. They send you 5, 10, 15, 20, 30.

statement: For the N-1 repeat messages the write still calls the database although the set already holds the sender, wasting network I/O and, more importantly, making the database handle those requests.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there is no changes happening in the DB, but you would still make a call to DB trying to write to the set.

statement: For each such write the database receives the request, reads the set, checks whether the entry exists, and discards it if it does (adds it if not) - a lot of work that changes nothing for the N-1 cases.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It would get the request. It would read the set, see if the entry exists in the set. It would discard.

statement: High-level pattern: whenever a database is doing a lot of unnecessary operations that lead to no state change, minimise them, because the database is the most brittle component - no matter which cloud provider you pick, if the database is down everything is down; protect it however you can.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: whenever you find a database that is doing a lot of unnecessary operations leading to no state changes in database, try to minimize them

statement: Protect the database like Voldemort protects the Deathly Hallows: keep it well protected by all the magical charms.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Keep it like well protected by all the magical charms

statement: Use an auxiliary database to minimise the unnecessary operations on the primary database: when a brittle component (typically the database) does many operations that change nothing, add an auxiliary database and reduce the load on the main one so the service stays up.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: how do we minimize it by using an auxiliary database? This is what I want to talk about.

statement: Adding the auxiliary database costs one more network I/O, but preventing the main database from going down by adding a bit of network cost is a good trade-off - worth it every single time.
detail: 'Network cost is not much in this case.' 'It's all about trade-off.'
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Preventing your main database from going down by adding a bit of network cost is a good trade-off to make.

statement: Auxiliary Redis write flow: the write first goes to the auxiliary Redis, which checks whether the entry (an unread message already exists from this sender) exists; if it exists, no write is made to the main database; if not, the write goes to the main database.
detail: Board: 'Auxiliary Redis' below the status update workers; 'workers will update the users in Redis as it gets the event'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Whenever the write happens, the write first happens into this Redis and it checks if the entry exists or not.

statement: With the auxiliary Redis the main database is not even called for the n-1 repeat messages; the auxiliary takes the bulk of those queries and all the hitting, while the main database is protected.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This way for n-1 times, you are not even calling this main DB, reducing the load on this database.

statement: Failure analysis: if the main database goes down everything is down anyway; if the auxiliary Redis goes down, all writes simply go to the main database, which handles the n-1 writes it was handling anyway - the auxiliary only sheds load.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So by adding this auxiliary database, you are just trying to shed the load that was there on this main database.

statement: With the auxiliary Redis, clearing the status (user clicks the message icon) must delete the entries from both the main Redis and the auxiliary Redis.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when you clear the status, it not only has to delete from here, but also delete from here.

statement: Keeping two databases may cause some glitches and slight inconsistency, but that is acceptable because unread-message counts are not transactional or money-related; the whole system being down, however, would be the end of the product.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's not something that deals with money and all, it just unread messages.

statement: Pick your battles: decide what you are trading off for what.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you need to pick your battles, what you are trading off for what.

statement: Next week (the teacher's personal favourite) is storage engines: the class builds its own storage engines - three of them, two of which go into granular details - to learn database internals and build intuition for writing your own database. Pre-reads will be shared; the recording is uploaded by about 3-4 o'clock.
detail: At closing the teacher repeated: next week dives into database details and implements a couple of other systems.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Next week is all about, it's my personal favorite week, storage engines, where we'll build our own storage engines.

statement: Knowing storage-engine internals builds intuition for how systems like Kafka work: the teacher did not know Kafka's internals, guessed them, and the guess was exactly how it was implemented; once intuition is built, 99% of such guesses are correct.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I didn't know internals of Kafka. I guessed it and it was exactly how it was implemented.

statement: A student proposed a cap: when a user has e.g. 10,000 messages, display '100+' instead, and once past that point stop writing to the Redis cluster since it no longer matters.
detail: Teacher: 'It does not matter.' 'True.' 'That's a good optimization.'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: if we have hundreds of 100 messages, then we only show that 100 plus.

statement: Threshold optimization: if the set length is already above a threshold (say 100), do not write even the first entry for a new sender, saving that extra write.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If this length is more than, let's say, 100, that's a threshold. You don't even write a first entry to this.

statement: Auxiliary Redis key model: instead of a set, it stores separate keys such as 'B received message from C' with value true (B_C: True), reducing the overhead of storing a set and comparing; storing it as a set also works - either way is fine.
detail: The teacher picked separate keys so the two Redis instances have clearly different key models.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: B received message from C, B received message from D as a key and value is just true.
flags: check: "anything." may be the end of Student 2's question

statement: The auxiliary Redis is for checking, not storing per message: if user B sends 10,000 messages, there is one write to the auxiliary Redis and one write to the main Redis, and every other message is only an existence check.
detail: The teacher's numbers were loose ('other 99 checks', 'I don't have to create 99999 entries over here').
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Not storing, I am just checking, checking, just checking, not storing.

statement: There is no count in the auxiliary Redis, only existence; a student had misunderstood it as incrementing a count there.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No, no, there is no count, there is no count over here. This is just existence.

statement: When the user clicks the message icon, the set and the auxiliary entries are deleted; when another message arrives, the entry is created again.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When another message was sent, then the entry would be created again.

statement: Failure case: if the write to one Redis succeeds and the write to the other fails, the two get out of sync; the worst that happens is the badge shows 2 while in reality there are 300 messages.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In case, let's say you wrote over here, but this [?write failed | asr: "right field"], or rather this [?write | asr: "right"] succeeded

statement: Accept a bit of inconsistency here: the system is not financial or critical, and introducing distributed transactions to keep both writes consistent is not worth the complexity.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But introducing that complexity of doing distributed transaction is not worth it.

statement: Making the status update transactional across the auxiliary Redis and the Redis cluster is not required: take some inconsistency in favour of high throughput; at worst you see a count of two while having three new senders, you will see all messages after clicking anyway, and a person who needs a reply will send another message - given how humans work, it is okay.
speaker: teacher
